title: III: The Recognition

teacherSummary.text: Hester sees a small, deformed stranger at the edge of the crowd, dressed partly in Native clothing; he recognizes her and signals her to be silent. He learns her story from a townsman. The Reverend John Wilson and the young minister Arthur Dimmesdale urge Hester to name the child's father. Dimmesdale pleads with emotion, but Hester refuses, and Wilson preaches on sin while she endures.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Speak, woman … Speak; and give your child a father” slowly and put it in my own words: Dimmesdale urges Hester to speak and name the father of her child. Next, craft. I notice the repeated command "Speak," spoken by the very man who is the father. The strongest word is “father”: it is the word that names his own secret. Then, effect. What is Dimmesdale asking of Hester in public, and why is it ironic? My answer: In public, Dimmesdale asks Hester to name her partner, and it is ironic because he is that partner; he asks her to reveal what he is too weak to confess, and her silence protects him.
